title: Mendelian genetics
note: Each organism carries two alleles per gene, which separate into different gametes (segregation). Genes on different chromosomes sort independently (independent assortment). For independent events, multiply probabilities; for mutually exclusive outcomes, add them.

read.title: Mendel's peas
text: In the 1850s and 1860s, Gregor Mendel crossed garden peas that bred true for contrasting traits, such as purple versus white flowers. All the first-generation (F1) offspring had purple flowers. White seemed to vanish. But when Mendel let the F1 plants self-fertilize, white flowers returned in about one quarter of the second generation. Across thousands of plants, the ratio of purple to white was close to 3:1.

Mendel explained this with units of inheritance that we now call genes. Each plant carries two copies, or alleles, one from each parent. The purple allele is dominant, so a plant with even one copy is purple. The white allele is recessive and shows only when a plant has two copies. When a plant makes gametes, its two alleles separate, so each gamete carries just one. This is the law of segregation.

A Punnett square shows the outcome of crossing two heterozygotes (Pp × Pp): one PP, two Pp, and one pp. Three of the four combinations look purple. Mendel then followed two traits at once and found they were inherited independently, giving a 9:3:3:1 ratio. We now know this holds for genes on different chromosomes, but not for genes close together on the same one.

q.q: Why did all F1 plants have purple flowers?
o: Purple is dominant and each F1 plant had one purple allele

q.q: What fraction of the F2 from Pp × Pp is expected to be white?

o: For genes close together on one chromosome
